And to the lustful: They have become horses mad after females (Jer 5:8). And of the pleasure-lovers: Do not cast your pearls before swine. And to the shameless: Nor give what is holy to dogs (Matt 7:6). And in common of them all: The vision of the four-footed beasts that were in the desert (Isa 30). The Lord therefore came, and did not find a man. For man, when he was in honor, did not understand: he was compared to senseless cattle, and became like them (Ps 48 [49]:13). I called them, he says, as a rational animal, and said: Incline your ear to the words of my mouth (Ps 77 [78]), and my people did not hear my voice. I cried out, and said: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). And in another place: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened (Matt 11:28). And there was none to hear; hence I said to them in the Gospel: You have neither seen the form of God, nor heard his voice, because you do not have his word abiding in you (John 5:37, 38).

According to the anagogy, at the rebuke of the Lord the sea becomes a desert when all the bitterness of this world is dried up, and the rivers are made desolate, of which the spiritual dragon in Egypt said: The rivers are mine, and I made them (Ezek 29:9). And of which we read in another place: What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers (Jer 2:18)? The fish too, when the net has been cast into the sea, shall rot, those which have been separated from the good fish.

No one who views things correctly thinks God possesses a physical body. It is only that the holy Scriptures speak in a human fashion about him. For those of us in simple and crass bodies can think in no other way, except that these things are adapted for us by a range of metaphors, so that in the perception of visible things we are able to know in part about the divine and higher being, which is higher than all bodily imaginings. Observe how in these words the message is adapted to human understanding.

Then he recalls for them what he has accomplished: "Behold, by my rebuke I will dry up the sea and make rivers a wilderness; and their fish shall be dried up because there is no water and shall die for thirst." Symmachus has rendered this passage as if it concerns events already accomplished: "Behold that at my rebuke I have dried up the sea, that I have made the rivers a desert and that their fish have been putrified for lack of water." Thus, the God of the universe accomplished this at the time he delivered them from the bondage of the Egyptians: it was then that he parted the Red Sea, divided the Jordan in two and revealed that the fish in its bed were dead from deprivation of its nourishing waters. If, however, one likewise understands this passage [to relate] to the future, as the Septuagint desires [to do], one will do no violence to the senses. It indicates from great miracles that he will also be able to accomplish small things: if it was easy for me to dry up the sea, he says, and to interrupt the course of rivers, it would have been much easier to annihilate an army that was marching against you.

I have many times endured your belief in idols and the infinite number of iniquities that you have perpetrated, but what you have dared now is not susceptible to any pardon: it is an evil that is irremediable and incurable. For I am no longer acting through the prophets as intermediaries, but I have assumed the form of a servant, and I have lived among you as a man; and in spite of the frequency of my appeals and my exhortations, I have not persuaded you. This, in turn, is confirmed by the recital of the divine Gospels in these terms: "Jesus cried out, saying, 'If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink,' and elsewhere: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." The divine Evangelists have let us know still many other declarations of this kind. In this way, then, the prophetic text has taught us that the total destruction that they undergo in the last place has been obtained for them by their folly against the Master. Then, in interrogative form again [he declares]: "Is not my hand strong to redeem? Or do I not have the strength to protect you [from danger]?" Do you think, he says, that the adversaries have conquered me because of my weakness? Is it not possible for anyone to see how easy and convenient it is for me to make you appear superior to everyone?

Third, he sets out the argument: because I came, through inspiration, I called, through the prophets: I called, and you refused (Prov 1:24).

Is my hand shortened? Here he excludes lack on the part of divine power, first excluding lack of power: shortened, that I cannot subject them to me even from afar; little, against the powerful, below: behold the hand of the Lord is not shortened (Isa 59:1).

Second, he sets out a sign of divine power: behold,

first, in the waters: at my rebuke, that is, my command, I will make the sea a desert, if I wish, as I did when Israel came forth from Egypt (Exod 14:15–31); I will turn the rivers into dry land, like the Arnon (Num 21:13–20) and the Jordan (Josh 4); the fishes shall rot, as in Exodus 7:16–21, when the waters were turned into blood: he rebuked the Red Sea and it was dried up (Ps 105[106]:9).

And as for what follows: I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and its covering shall be as haircloth, either let us understand by heaven all that is above us, as the birds which are in the air are called heavenly, and the adverse powers, which run to and fro between heaven and earth, are said to be heavenly. Or certainly the heaven is clothed with darkness when it is covered with clouds. According to what is written: Who covers the heaven with clouds, and gives rain to the earth (Ps 146 [147]:8). And in threatening drought God says: I will make the heaven bronze, and the earth iron (Deut 28:23). Not that the nature of the elements is changed, but that by bronze and iron the greatness of the punishments is shown. The philosophers say that the clouds are not raised up more than ten stadia from the earth, and hide the brightness of the sun. It is not, then, the heaven that is wrapped in sackcloth, but, the light of heaven being shut off, the air that is beneath is darkened by the darkness of the cloud. We can interpret the heavens wrapped in darkness and covered with sackcloth thus: that we say all are under sin, and that the saints too need the mercy of God.

Yes! creation itself bewailed its Lord: for the sun was darkened, and the rocks were rent, and the very temple assumed the garb of mourners, for its "veil was rent from the top to the bottom." And this is what God signified to us by the voice of Isaiah, saying, "And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and wrap it around with sackcloth."
Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

"I will clothe the sky with shadows, and I will change its cover to be like mourning cloth." He has done this and will do it. For he did it when he was crucified: "From the sixth hour to the ninth the shadows covered the whole earth." And he will do it again at the time of the fulfillment, for it says, "The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give off its light."
Second, he shows signs of his power in the heavens: I will clothe the aerial heavens with darkness, as in Egypt (Exod 10:21); who covers the heaven with clouds (Ps 146[147]:8).

For the power of His strong word, by which He always confuted the Pharisees and Scribes, and, in short, all your nation's teachers that questioned Him, had a cessation like a plentiful and strong spring, the waters of which have been turned off, when He kept silence, and chose to return no answer to any one in the presence of Pilate; as has been declared in the memoirs of His apostles, in order that what is recorded by Isaiah might have efficacious fruit, where it is written, "The Lord gives me a tongue, that I may know when I ought to speak." Again, when He said, "Thou art my God; be not far from me," He taught that all men ought to hope in God who created all things, and seek salvation and help from Him alone; and not suppose, as the rest of men do, that salvation can be obtained by birth, or wealth, or strength, or wisdom.

"The Lord God has given me the tongue of the doctrine." These words refer to Christ as well, who preached his new doctrine to all the peoples. And therefore all the peoples listened to it and were converted.

Now what ought we to learn before everything else, but to be silent that we may be able to speak? Lest my voice should condemn me before that of another acquits me, for it is written: "By your words you shall be condemned." What need is there, then, that you should hasten to undergo the danger of condemnation by speaking when you can be more safe by keeping silent? How many have I seen to fall into sin by speaking, but scarcely one by keeping silent; and so it is more difficult to know how to keep silent than how to speak … a person is wise, then, who knows how to keep silent. Lastly, the Wisdom of God said, "The Lord has given to me the tongue of learning, that I should know when it is good to speak." Justly, then, is one wise who has received of the Lord to know when he ought to speak. Wherefore the Scripture says well: "A wise person will keep silence until there is opportunity."
On the Duties of the Clergy 1.2.5

The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain by a word him who is weary. He rouses in the morning, in the morning he rouses my ear, that I may hear him as a master. The Lord God has opened my ear: and I do not gainsay; I have not gone backward. I gave my body to those who struck, and my cheeks to those who plucked them. I did not turn away my face from those who rebuked and spat. The Lord God is my helper, therefore I am not confounded: therefore I have set my face like a very hard rock, and I know that I shall not be confounded. LXX: The Lord gives me a tongue of discipline, that I may know when I ought to speak a word. He set me in the morning, he added to me an ear for hearing; and the discipline of the Lord opens my ears. But I do not refuse, nor do I gainsay. I gave my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to blows. But I did not turn away my face from the shame of spittings. And the Lord is my helper, therefore I am not confounded: but I have set my face like a very strong rock, and I shall know that I shall not be confounded. The Jews, separating this little chapter from what goes before, want to refer it to the person of Isaiah: that he says he received from the Lord the word by which to sustain the weary and wandering people and call it back to salvation; and that, after the manner of little children, who are taught in the morning hours, he hears from the Holy Spirit what he should speak; and that he did not gainsay his command, but when the Lord asked, Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? he answered him: Here am I, send me (Isa 6:8). And because he had said, Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom: give ear to the Law of our God, you people of Gomorrah (Isa 1:10), he suffered such hard things that he was exposed not only to insulting words but also to the pains of blows. Yet, through his awareness of the God who commanded him, he was not at all terrified; but, according to what is said to Ezekiel, Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like adamant and flint I have made your face (Ezek 3:8, 9), he beat down all their assaults. So let those say who strive by every means to overturn the prophecies about Christ and to twist them by a crooked interpretation into a perverse understanding: as if, should these things too have been written of Isaiah, they could take away the other testimonies about Christ, which are so plain that they pour their clear light into the eyes of all. To the person of the Lord, then, with whom the previous book also ended, these things too are to be referred: that according to the dispensation of the body he assumed he was taught, and received a tongue of discipline, that he might know when he ought to speak and when to be silent. Indeed, he who was silent in his passion now speaks through the Apostles and apostolic men in the whole world. And it belongs to great knowledge to give one's fellow servants their food in due season, and to consider the persons of the hearers. Hence the Apostle Paul too speaks to those who did not accept the faith of the Prophets with testimonies from their own authors: as some of your own poets have said: For we are also his offspring (Acts 17:28), meaning Aratus. And again, from the Comic poet: Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor 15:33); and the hexameter verse of Epimenides: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies (Titus 1:12). If these do not keep the order and measure of the meter in translation, it must be known that in Greek they run on metrical feet. And he did this because he had received a tongue of discipline, that he might know when he ought to speak a word. To him an ear was added by grace, which he did not have by nature: so that we may understand that by no means are the ears of the body to be taken here, but those of the mind, of which the Lord also spoke in the Gospel: He who has ears to hear, let him hear (Luke 8:8). This discipline and instruction opened his ears, that he might pass on the knowledge of the Father even to us; he who did not gainsay him, but became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil 2). So that he set his body, or his back, to the blows; and scourges cut the breast that held God, and he did not turn his cheeks away from the slaps. That he endured this from the servant of the chief of the Priests is not in doubt, so that the crowds of the Jews too mocked him, vying with one another. Struck and spat upon, he did not blush, but was led as a lamb to the sacrifice; and as a sheep before its shearer he did not open his mouth. And that the Son, according to the mystery of the body he took up, heard from the Father what he should speak, we learn more fully in the Gospel, in which he himself says: And the Father who sent me has given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak. And again: As I hear, so I judge (John 8:28; 5:30).

And so learn from your own experience to sympathize with those in trouble, and never to terrify with destructive despair those who are in danger, nor harden them with severe speeches, but rather restore them with gentle and kindly consolations, and as the wise Solomon says, "Spare not to deliver those who are led forth to death, and to redeem those who are to be slain," and after the example of our Saviour, break not the bruised reed, nor quench the smoking flax, and ask of the Lord that grace, by means of which you yourself may faithfully learn both in deed and power to sing: "the Lord hath given me a learned tongue that I should know how to uphold by word him that is weary:" for no one could bear the devices of the enemy, or extinguish or repress those carnal fires which burn with a sort of natural flame, unless God's grace assisted our weakness, or protected and supported it.
Second Conference of Abbot Moses, Chapter 13

[Ministers] who sing thankful hymns say that they have been given a tongue of discipline; that is, they are able to speak in a trained manner and expound the divine mysteries without fault and are able to speak fittingly to those who need words of encouragement.… On us the sun of righteousness has arisen and has shed its light on our mind so that we are and are known as children of light and of the day. For we, having faith in Christ, are enriched with illumination from him; that is, we have our hearing enhanced and are thus enabled to hear.

Christ our Master says this in a human way. For the rest, we find many statements of this kind in the divine Gospels: "And Jesus increased in age," it is said, "and wisdom and grace before God and before people." He calls youth "early"; thus, the prophet likewise taught this in a preceding passage. After having announced [Christ's] conception by the Virgin, he had added, "Before he [the child] shall know good or evil, he refuses evil, to choose the good." The Evangelist declares something similar: "And the child grew and became strong in spirit, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was on him." As for the phrase "the instruction the Lord gives opens my ears," in my opinion, it is not pronounced regarding him but on the subject of the disciples who believed in [Christ], for he gives the name of "ears" to his hearers, that is, to those to whom he presents the divine words, that is, to those to whom he declared, as we learn it in reading the holy Gospels: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear!"

The Lord has given me. Here he gives himself as an example.

And first, as to the grace of the benefit he received, both as to eloquence: a learned tongue, that I should know how to uphold, with encouragements: your words have confirmed them that were staggering (Job 4:4); and as to wisdom: he wakens my ear, to listen, in the morning, from the beginning of my preaching, or from the beginning of his life, or because he was then alone to pray: I will meditate on you in the morning (Ps 62:7[63:6]).

For how shall patience be looked for, if there be not previously labours and sorrows? Or how can fortitude be tested with no assault from enemies? Or how shall magnanimity be exhibited, unless after contumely and injustice? Or how can long-suffering be proved, unless there has first been the calumny of Antichrist? And, finally, how can a man behold virtue with his eyes, unless the iniquity of the very wicked has previously appeared? Thus even our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ comes before us, when He would shew men how to suffer, Who when He was smitten bore it patiently, being reviled He reviled not again, when He suffered He threatened not, but He gave His back to the smiters, and His cheeks to buffetings, and turned not His face from spitting; and at last, was willingly led to death, that we might behold in Him the image of all that is virtuous and immortal, and that we, conducting ourselves after these examples, might truly tread on serpents and scorpions, and on all the power of the enemy.

And so it is shewn to all that the Body was not the Word, but Body of the Word. And it was this that Thomas handled when it had risen from the dead, and saw in it the print of the nails, which the Word Himself had undergone, seeing them fixed in His own Body, and though able to prevent it, did not do so. On the contrary, the incorporeal Word made His own the properties of the Body, as being His own Body. Why, when the Body was struck by the attendant, as suffering Himself He asked, ‘Why smitest thou Me?’ And being by nature intangible, the Word yet said, ‘I gave My back to the stripes, and My cheeks to blows, and hid not My face from shame and spitting.’ For what the human Body of the Word suffered, this the Word, dwelling in the body, ascribed to Himself, in order that we might be enabled to be partakers of the Godhead of the Word. And verily it is strange that He it was Who suffered and yet suffered not. Suffered, because His own Body suffered, and He was in it, which thus suffered; suffered not, because the Word, being by Nature God, is impassible. And while He, the incorporeal, was in the passible Body, the Body had in it the impassible Word, which was destroying the infirmities inherent in the Body. But this He did, and so it was, in order that Himself taking what was ours and offering it as a sacrifice, He might do away with it, and conversely might invest us with what was His, and cause the Apostle to say: ‘This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality.’

If you remain unruffled, you silence your insolent assailant by giving him a practical illustration of self-control. Were you struck? So also was the Lord. Were you spat on? The Lord also suffered this, for "he did not turn his face from the shame of the spittle." … You have not been condemned to death or crucified.
HOMILY AGAINST THOSE WHO ARE PRONE TO ANGER

[This is] as though he were to say, "Though I knew beforehand that they would strike me, I did not even turn aside my cheek; for how could I have nerved my disciples to undergo death for the truth if I had been afraid?"

Now if God willed to accept and to lower Himself to such sufferings, dishonours, and humiliations, then no matter how much you humble yourself, you whose nature is mud and subject to death, you will never resemble your Lord [in this]. God for your sake humbled Himself, but you, for your own sake, do not humble yourself. You are proud and puffed up. God came and took up your burden to give you His rest, but you do not wish to endure labours and suffering. By your labours your wounds are healed.

What do I mean by this, hold fast to Christ? It was for this reason that He chose to suffer on earth Himself. Ye have heard, while the prophet was being read, how He “did not turn away His back from the smiters, and His face from the spittings of men,” how “He turned not His cheek from their hands;” wherefore chose He to suffer all these things, but that He might console the suffering? He could have raised His flesh at the last day: but then thou wouldest not have had thy ground of hope, since thou hadst not seen Him. He deferred not His resurrection, that thou mightest not still be in doubt. Suffer then tribulation in the world with the same end as that which thou hast observed in Christ: and let not those who do evil, and flourish in this life, move thee.

This whole recital is taught by the holy Gospels. For the servant of the high priest gave [Christ] a blow on the cheek; some struck his face, saying, "Prophesy to us, Christ! Who is the one who struck you?" Others spat in his face; as for Pilate, he had him scourged and delivered him to be crucified. So, all this he predicts in the prophecy to teach of his own patience.

He also sets out the constancy of his obedience, that he did not abandon his obedience for any danger: I have given my body, that is, I exposed myself that I should suffer such things; or perhaps he literally suffered these things, but in Christ this was completely fulfilled (Matthew 26 and 27): I have given my dear soul into the hand of enemies (Jer 12:7).

Nevertheless, you will say, adversity is a terrible thing and grievous to be borne. Yet look at it again compared with another image and then also learn to despise it. For the railings, and insults, and reproaches, and gibes inflicted by enemies, and their plots are compared to a worn-out garment, and moth-eaten wool when God says "Fear ye not the reproach of men, neither be ye afraid of their revilings, for they shall wax old as doth a garment, and like moth-eaten wool so shall they be consumed." Therefore let none of these things which are happening trouble thee, but ceasing to invoke the aid of this or that person, and to run after shadows (for such are human alliances), do thou persistently call upon Jesus, whom thou servest, merely to bow his head; and in a moment of time all these evils will be dissolved.

And the Father was Christ's helper. For he did not allow or concede that his own Son should be completely shamed or overwhelmed. For they were punished, those who sought to take their punishment out on me as those who dare to fight with God.… For though being with us, he was the only-begotten Word of God. He put on an identical human likeness, by which reason alone he was believed to be of a nature with us. For every human being is subject to faults and sins, and no one alive is completely blameless. He alone in becoming man retained the divine dignity.… And being Word and God, his flesh was able to shoo away destruction. Thus, the Son became a man who was fit to be accepted by the Father. For all that human beings have is God-given. For the one God and Father, through him, undid the power of death through his resurrection from the dead.… He was the servant of God, who while being human was yet truly the Son of God and the Father. And to hear his voice means no transgression of the law but a confirming of the law through types and shadows discerning the truth which is Christ and the prophecies of him, as Paul notes. … His voice is the evangelical and divine preaching that calls us to the redemption that is through faith in Christ. He also calls us to a proper behavior that lives in a way that is, by far, more consistent than the way of the law. The law was given in the shadows. Faith was given in the bright and shining light.

Near is he who justifies me: who gainsays me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord God is my helper: who is he that will condemn me? Behold, they shall all be worn away like a garment, the moth shall eat them. LXX: He who is near justifies me: who is he that is judged with me, let him resist me together? And who is he that enters into judgment against me? Let him draw near to me. Behold, the Lord is my helper, who will afflict me? Behold, all of you shall grow old like a garment, and like a moth it shall eat you. If anyone, he says, thinks that I was justly given over to the cross and had committed some sin, let him resist me. Who is he that is judged with me, so that he may be overcome not by the power of my majesty but by reason? Now a man is judged with the Lord not by the authority of one who reigns but by comparison of virtues: as the Apostles also judge the twelve tribes of Israel, and the Ninevites and the queen of Sheba judge the people of the Jews. In this sense it is said to Jerusalem: Sodom is justified by you (Ezek 16:52).

Third, he assigns the reason for this security from the power of the one who helps him: he is near that justifies me, namely, God. Who will contend with me, with words; let us stand together: set me beside you, O Lord, and let any man's hand fight against me (Job 17:3); who is my adversary, with deeds.

There is a person who runs down birth, describing it as subject to decay and death, who forces things and suggests that the Savior was speaking about having children in saying that we should not store treasure on earth, where it grows rusty and moth-eaten. And [this person] is not ashamed to set alongside these the prophet's words: "You shall all grow old like clothes, and the moth will feed on you." We do not contradict Scripture. Our bodies are subject to decay and are naturally unstable. Perhaps he might be prophesying decay to his audience because they were sinners. The Savior was not speaking about having children. He was encouraging sharing of resources in those who wanted only to amass vast amounts of wealth rather than offer help to those in need.

Since, then, no one can be justified in the presence of the Lord, all shall grow old like a garment (Ps 101 [102]). And what grows old is near to perishing. And like a moth, he says, it shall eat them: namely the conscience of sins, and jealousy over the nations that have been saved. Of this it is said at the end of this volume: Their worm shall not die. And in Micah, against the perverse princes: I will take away their goods like a moth that eats them up, and walks upon the rule in the day of watching (Mic 7:4 LXX). And in Proverbs: An understanding heart is a moth of the bones (Prov 14:30 LXX). For moth in the present place Symmachus translated rust, Aquila worm.

"Behold, you will all like a garment grow old, and something like a worm will devour you." The parable is accurate, for the worm that comes from the clothes destroys them, and sin, which is born from us, ruins those who allow it to grow.

Isaiah also gives the name "moth" to those who devour their conscience in their recklessness.… It might be said that the moths are their sins, which worm their way in among those they inhabit, like moths devouring clothing for food. An attitude that inclines toward having no fear is indicative of a people on their way to this kind of ruin, yet who think they are indestructible. But punishment also clearly awaits them. They will be utterly consumed by misfortune as by a moth.

Who is he that shall condemn me, with false judgments: God is he that justifies: who is he that shall condemn? (Rom 8:33–34);

again, he assigns the reason for this security from the weakness of those who attack him: lo, they shall all be destroyed as a garment, with old age, in which is signified natural defect, the moth, in which is signified the violent man: who am to be consumed as rottenness, and as a garment that is moth-eaten (Job 13:28); as if to say: from all these things, just as I, after the benefits I received, obey God and trust in him, so should you also.

By the mouth of Isaiah also [God] has asked concerning him, "Who is there among you that hears God? Let him hear the voice of his Son." When, therefore, he here presents him with the words, "This is my beloved Son," this clause is of course understood, "who I have promised." For if he once promised and afterwards says, "This is he," it is suitable conduct for one who accomplishes his purpose that he should utter his voice in proof of the promise that he had formerly made; but unsuitable in one who is amenable to the retort, "Can you, indeed, have a right to say, 'This is my son,' concerning whom you have given us no previous information, any more than you have favored us with a revelation about your own prior existence?"

Who among you fears the Lord, hearing the voice of his servant? He who has walked in darkness and has no light, let him hope in the name of the Lord, and lean upon his God. LXX: Who is there among you that fears the Lord, let him hearken to the voice of his child: those who walk in darkness have no light. Trust in the name of the Lord, and lean upon God. You scourged me, you spat upon my face: yet I call my persecutors to repentance. For I do not will the death of the sinful people, but only that it turn back and live (Ezek 33). And I say: who is there among you that fears the Lord and hears the voice of the servant, or child, that is, of his Son? Of these the one belongs to the flesh he assumed, the other to his nature. Nor let us think it a small thing to fear the Lord, according to what is said in Proverbs: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10). For perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and he who fears is not perfect in love. But here fear is put for timidity, and εὐλαβείᾳ, of which we also read elsewhere: Blessed is he who fears all things (Prov 28:14), on account of εὐλάβειαν, that is, on account of timidity: those whom people commonly call God-fearing in the religion of God. For the Lord protects their path, and guards the way of the God-fearing. Of this fear it is written: The fear of the Lord surpasses all things. And elsewhere: There is no want for those who fear him (Sir 25:14; Ps 33 [34]:10). Indeed, it is only after many steps of virtue that one arrives at such fear of the Lord. For the divine word speaks in the person of a master and father, instructing a disciple and a son: If you call upon wisdom, and give your voice to understanding, and if you seek her like money, and search her out like treasures: then you shall understand the fear of the Lord, and find the knowledge of God (Prov 2:3). This is the fear that keeps the souls of the saints whole, chaste and pure, of which it is said: The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever. To it the divine oracles exhort us: Fear the Lord, and give him glory (Rev 14:7). Let him, then, who so fears the Lord hear the voice of his servant, or child, who walked in darkness, and there was no light for him; who had no form nor glory, but in the likeness of sinful flesh took the form of a servant, that he might overcome sin in the flesh. Of him it is said that he should hope in the name of the Lord and lean upon his God, so that whatever belongs to human frailty he may strengthen and sustain by the divine majesty. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy it is said of sinners, who would not obey the voice of his Son, and walk in the darkness of error, and therefore have no light. For it could not be that wisdom should enter into a perverse soul. They neither knew nor understood, and therefore they walk in darkness. For they did not do the works and commandments of the Lord, nor sow righteousness for themselves, nor gather the vintage of the vine, so as to kindle for themselves the light of knowledge. For he who desires wisdom, let him keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to him. Hence it is also said to God: Your precepts are light. And elsewhere: The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes (Ps 18 [19]:9). And the ungodly are commanded to trust in the Lord, and, falling through their sins, to lean upon his help and be sustained by it.

It is as a man that he calls himself "Servant," for "although he exists in the form of God, he has assumed the form of a servant." Likewise in the divine Gospel [Christ] says that he has received instruction as to what he should say and proclaim. "They walk in darkness, and there is no light for them." Although the light has risen, as for them, they have clung to the darkness. "Trust in the name of the Lord, and rely on God." [Isaiah] says, if you really put absolute and true hope in God, that will [serve to] sustain you and make you sure.

If then this is the character of the body that rises from the dead, let us now see what is the meaning of the threatened "eternal fire." Now we find in the prophet Isaiah that the fire by which each person is punished is described as belonging to himself. For it says, "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves." These words seem to indicate that every sinner kindles for himself the flame of his own fire and is not plunged into a fire that has been previously kindled by someone else or that existed before him.

That "fire" is not "from the altar". The fire which is "from the altar" is the fire of the Lord; but that which is outside the altar is not the Lord's, but is the proper fire of each one of those who sin, of which it is said: "their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished". That "fire" therefore is of those very ones who kindled it, as also elsewhere it is written: "walk in your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves". But to Isaiah not his own fire is applied, but the fire of the altar, which will "purge around" his "lips".

One light alone let us shun: that which is the offspring of the terrible fire. Let us not walk in the light of our own fire and in the very flame we have kindled. For I know of a cleansing fire that Christ came to send on the earth, and that he himself is anagogically called a fire. This Fire takes away whatever is material and of evil habit. This he desires to kindle with all speed, for he longs for speed in doing us good, since he gives us even coals of fire to help us. I know also a fire that is not cleansing but avenging; either that fire of Sodom, which he pours down on all sinners, mingled with brimstone and storms, or that which is prepared for the devil and his angels.

Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames that you have kindled: by my hand this has been done to you; you shall sleep in sorrows. LXX: Behold, all of you kindle a fire and strengthen the flame; walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame that you have kindled; because of me these things have been done to you. You shall sleep in grief. Exhortation profits nothing, nor is there hope of salvation after crimes. All have turned aside, together they have become useless (Ps 13 [14]); all kindle a fire for themselves and strengthen the flame. For they have in themselves hay, wood, stubble, thorns and thistles and darnel, which are to be handed over to the eternal burning. Hence it is also written in Proverbs: In much wood the fire thrives (Prov 25:21). But if a little fire lays hold of great material, how much will a great flame lay waste? It is said also in the Epistle that is ascribed to the Hebrews, of the earth that, bringing forth thorns and thistles, is reprobate and near to a curse, and its end is burning (Heb 6:8). Therefore those who are girded and surrounded with flames, and have strengthened the burning for themselves, are called to salvation, and it is said to them: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flames that you have kindled, that in punishments and torments they may learn the power of God and return to salvation. And it signifies the devastation of the Jewish people, by which they were handed over to the Romans, and they bear the yoke of captivity to this day. For by the hand of Christ all these things were done, and they shall sleep in grief and sorrows, because neither through benefits nor through torments would they receive the Son of God. Hence he speaks to them: Go into the eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt 25:41). This is what the Apostle also says: For wrath has come upon you to the end (1 Thess 2:16). From this little chapter we learn that each one kindles a fire for himself according to the quality of his sin. And just as, of people staying in the same place and, if one may say so, in the same bed, some are healthy while others burn with the heat of fevers, feeling different torments from the diversity of their humors and phlegm: so the fire that is kindled by sinners has its fuel in sins and in iniquity, of which it is written: Iniquity shall burn like a fire, and shall be devoured by burning like dry grass (Isa 9:18).

Moreover, what we have set down according to the Seventy: A man who is estranged from me and sets his thoughts in his heart, and the torment (or punishment) of his iniquity before his face, agrees with that testimony which is written in Isaiah: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled; for each one kindles for himself the blazing of flames and prepares punishments for himself, while he is unwilling to correct his errors by repentance, but remains in errors that deserve the burning of flames.

It is impious to blame God's severity for our misfortunes: we should instead accuse ourselves. For when we commit the sins that cause our torture, we are ourselves the authors of our torments. Why then do we complain of the bitterness of our punishments? Each one of us punishes himself.

This is why the prophet said to us: "Behold, all ye that kindle a fire, that have added fuel to the flame; walk in the light of your fire and in the sparks that ye have kindled." For the whole human race is rushing headlong into eternal punishment by the very course that the Scriptures describe. First we kindle the fire, then add fuel to the flames, and lastly enter the flames that we have prepared. When does man first kindle eternal fire for himself? Surely when he first begins to sin. But when does he add fuel to the flames? When he heaps up sins upon sins. When shall he enter the everlasting fire? When he has already completed the irrevocable account of wickedness by the increase of his sins, as our Savior said to the leaders of the Jews: "Fill ye up then the measure of your fathers, ye serpents, ye generation of vipers," The men whom the Lord himself told to fill up the measure were not far from completing the full number of their sins. Because they were no longer worthy of salvation, they filled up the number of iniquities by which they were to perish. Whence also, when the ancient Law recalled that the sins of the Amorreans were fulfilled, it is said that the angels spoke to the blessed Lot, saying: "Whomsoever thou hast in the city, bring them out of this place, because the cry of them is waxen great before the face of the Lord, and the Lord hath sent us to destroy them." For a long time, truly, that most sinful people had been kindling the fires by which they perished, and so when the tale of their iniquities was completed they burned in the flames of their own crimes. For they deserved so ill of God that they suffered in this world the Gehenna that is to come in the later judgment.
On the Government of God, Book 4, Chapter 8

As all things, are subject to sacred authority and the will of God rules everything, whatever evils and whatever punishments we bear daily are the censure of his divine hand, which censure, indeed, we constantly arouse and kindle by our sins. We kindle the fire of the celestial wrath and arouse the flames by which we are burned, so that the words of the prophet may rightly be used against us as often as we endure such ills: "Make your way into the flames of the fire that you have kindled.'' From this we see that according to the sacred sentence each sinner is preparing for himself the suffering that he endures. None of our misfortunes can be imputed to God; we are the authors of our own misery. For God is gracious and merciful and, as the Scripture says, he wishes no one to perish or be injured. So whatever is done against us is done by our own actions; there is nothing more cruel to us than ourselves; we, I say, are torturing ourselves even against God's will.

But, forsooth, I seem to be contradicting myself; whereas I said before that we are punished by God on account of our sins, now I say that we are punishing ourselves. Both are true; we are indeed punished by God, but we ourselves force him to punish us. Inasmuch as we cause our own punishment, who can doubt that we are chastising ourselves by our crimes? For whoever gives cause for his punishment chastises himself, according to the saying: "Every one is bound by the chains of his sins." If wicked men are bound by the chains of their sins, every sinner doubtless binds himself when he sins.
On the Government of God, Book 8, Chapter 1
51: Hear me, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut out. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you: for I called him alone, and blessed him, and multiplied him. The Lord therefore will comfort Zion, and will comfort all her ruins, and will make her desert like delights, and her wilderness like the garden of the Lord. Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise. LXX: Hear, you who pursue what is just, and seek the Lord. Look to the strong rock which you hewed out, and to the hole of the pit which you dug. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you, for he was one, and I called him, and blessed him, and loved him, and multiplied him: and now I will comfort you, Zion. And I have comforted all her deserts like a paradise, and the things that are toward the west like the paradise of the Lord: they shall find exultation and gladness in her, confession and the voice of praise. While those who kindled a fire for themselves and made the flames most strong sleep in grief and everlasting sorrow, you who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord (and he means the choir of the Apostles and of those who believed through the Apostles), look to the rock, that is, to Abraham your father, from whom you were hewn, and to the cavern of the pit from which you were cut out, that is, to Sarah who bore you. And consider this: that when he was a hundred years old and one, and had a barren wife, I multiplied his sons like the stars of heaven, so that their multitude surpassed number. If, then, from one man so many thousands of peoples were born, what great thing is it for me to restore the ruins of Zion, and to change her deserts into a paradise of pleasure, and into the garden of the Lord which God planted in Eden toward the East; and that there should be found in her, in place of the various trees, joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise? The Jews refer this to the times of Zerubbabel, because after the devastation of Babylon Zion was restored, the Temple built, and the ancient religion given back. But just as above (Isa 49:22, 23) it is said to Zion: They shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nurses; and: Behold, these shall come from afar, and those from the north and the sea, and these from the land of the south; when Zion shall say: The place is too narrow for me: make room for me that I may dwell: things which exclude the meanness of those times, and are not known to have been fulfilled in the earthly Jerusalem: so here too the Lord speaks to those who pursue what is just, according to what is said elsewhere: Seek peace, and pursue it (Ps 33 [34]:15); and again: Pursuing hospitality (Rom 12:13). And they seek the Lord, so that one may infer things present from things former: since far more difficult things have already been done, let them not doubt that these things which are promised will come to pass. Further, according to the Seventy it is said to the pursuers of righteousness that they should look to the most strong rock which they hewed out, and the hole of the pit which they dug, that is, to the Lord the Savior, of whom the Apostle speaks: And the rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4). And elsewhere it is written: He set my feet upon a rock (Ps 39 [40]:3). And again: On a rock he exalted me. For they pierced his side with a lance, and from it came out blood and water; and they dug his hands and feet, as the Lord the Savior himself says: They dug my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones (Ps 21 [22]:18). We can call the hewn rock the tomb of the Savior, in which he was laid, and, rising from the dead, he begot innumerable sons. And he was called Abraham, that is, father of many nations. Just as Sarah, at first barren, is understood as the Church, which by another name is called Zion, whom the Lord has comforted, and whose deserts he has made like a paradise. For more are the children of the desolate than of her who has a husband. And what is said, And the things that are toward the West I will make into the paradise of the Lord, or into the garden of God, signifies that on those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death a sudden light has arisen. For paradise, in whose place we rendered delights, the Hebrew has EDEN (עדן), of which it is written at the beginning of Genesis. And this is to be noted, that in Zion, which is compared to the paradise of God, there ought to be nothing else but joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise, so that what the saints will do in heaven with the Angels of God, this they may practice on earth too in the unceasing praise of the Lord.

"Righteous," he says, instead of "righteousness," which is through Christ through faith in him, a faith that justifies the ungodly and removes all stain from those who have been filthy, and cleanses them in the Spirit and prepares for them the shining honor of sonship. They pursue righteousness, not in the sense of driving it before them and so away from their minds, but of running toward it to take hold of it. As David said, "Seek peace and pursue it." … The speech of the holy prophets always draws figures from the visible and the tangible things. For it has expressions that transcend reference, the senses and even the mind. In this way "Zion" is mentioned—not that we think of the earthly city but rather take it to be the spiritual one, that is, the church of the living God. Or how else would we see the words of the prophet coming true?…"Worship in spirit and truth," and the power of spiritual worship gave off the pleasant spiritual fragrance and joy in the hope that is in Christ. For if we trust that our body of lowliness will be transformed into the body of his glory, so we shall be with him and reign with him, assembled among the children of God and enriched with his divine and life-giving Spirit. We too bring forward the spiritual harvest to him—the confession and hymns of thanksgiving. For with such sacrifices is God well pleased.

For the divine voice says somewhere in the prophecy of Isaiah, "Consider Abraham, your father, and Sarah, who gave you birth." Scripture gives this admonition to those who wander outside virtue. Just as at sea those who are carried away from the direction of the harbor bring themselves back on a course by a clear sign, on seeing either a beacon light raised up high or some mountain peak coming into view, in the same way Scripture by the example of Abraham and Sarah may guide again to the harbor of the divine will those adrift on the sea of life with a pilotless mind.

He is leaving aside the unbelievers here in order to address those who have believed: it is to them that he gives the name of enamored with God and with righteousness. He comforts them because they are few in number and invites them to turn their eyes toward their ancestors: he reminds them of Abraham and Sarah and the many thousands of descendants who came from them. This is similar to the term expressed in the divine Gospels: "Do not fear, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom." It is the same here.

Nothing made is an obstacle to my power: not the fact that I called just one man or that old age was on him, or that Sarah lacked the physical capability; yet his race was [indeed] increased, just as I had wished. Be unbelieving no longer, therefore, even though you are [now] easy to count; I will make you too many to number.

923. Concerning the second, he does three things.

First, he gives an example: look unto the rock, namely, Abraham, because of his old age, whence you are hewn, as though violently, not according to the course of nature; and to the hole of the pit, namely, Sarah, to whom it had ceased to be after the manner of women (Gen 18:11): neither did he consider his own body, when it was already dead (Rom 4:19), in which is shown that God has power to make fertile; for I called him alone (cf. Gen 12:1): Abraham was one (Ezek 33:24).

It is not a question of inhabited places but of desert places, not of regions situated in the east but of those in the west. Those who have seen the city with their own eyes know that the temple of the Jews was in the eastern part of the city, whereas the cross and the [place of] the resurrection were in the western part. Moreover, these places were formerly situated outside the walls. The divine apostle was witness to this when he said, "Jesus … suffered outside the gate. Therefore let us go forth to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach." He makes this prediction accordingly: all the places of the city that were deserted and all those that were in the west will be as the garden of the Lord, for they truly possess the tree of life. "They shall find in it gladness and exultation, thanksgiving and the voice of praise." This also we still see fulfilled in our day: in place of the smoke, of the odor of fat that rises from the victims and of the cult rendered according to the law, which the Lord of the universe, even in former days, did not find agreeable, night and day Zion raises hymns in honor of the God of the universe, for it is filled with [worshipers] who chant hymns.

For the law promulgated on Horeb is now old, and belongs to yourselves alone; but this is for all universally. Now, law placed against law has abrogated that which is before it, and a covenant which comes after in like manner has put an end to the previous one; and an eternal and final law-namely, Christ-has been given to us, and the covenant is trustworthy, after which there shall be no law, no commandment, no ordinance. Have you not read this which Isaiah says: "Hearken unto Me, hearken unto Me, my people; and, ye kings, give ear unto Me: for a law shall go forth from Me, and My judgment shall be for a light to the nations. My righteousness approaches swiftly, and My salvation shall go forth, and nations shall trust in Mine arm?" And by Jeremiah, concerning this same new covenant, He thus speaks: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers, in the day that I took them by the hand, to bring them out of the land of Egypt." If, therefore, God proclaimed a new covenant which was to be instituted, and this for a light of the nations, we see and are persuaded that men approach God, leaving their idols and other unrighteousness, through the name of Him who was crucified, Jesus Christ, and abide by their confession even unto death, and maintain piety. Moreover, by the works and by the attendant miracles, it is possible for all to understand that He is the new law, and the new covenant, and the expectation of those who out of every people wait for the good things of God. For the true spiritual Israel, and descendants of Judah, Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham (who in uncircumcision was approved of and blessed by God on account of his faith, and called the father of many nations), are we who have been led to God through this crucified Christ, as shall be demonstrated while we proceed.

"Listen to me, my people, and give ear to me, my nation; for a law will go forth from me." And how could it go forth now, if it were the same law that went forth in the days of Moses? But it is evident that here he mystically signifies the spiritual law, which is the New Testament. "And my justice is a light to the peoples," that is, my sacrament. He also means that the conscience of the Gentiles, which is now clouded by idolatry, will be enlightened after all their gods are condemned by the divine sentence.

Attend to me, my people, and my tribe, hear me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment shall rest for a light of the peoples. Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth: and my arms shall judge the peoples. The islands shall wait for me, and shall wait upon my arm. LXX: Hear me, hear me, my people, and kings, attend to me: for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations. My righteousness draws near swiftly, and my salvation shall go forth like a light: and in my arm shall the nations hope. The islands shall wait for me, and in my arm they shall hope. Once in the Hebrew it is said, Attend; twice according to the Seventy, hear me, hear me: to teach us that we ought to hear both with the ears of the body and with the sense of the soul. And the multitude of the nations, which is the people of God, is called to listen carefully to what is said; of which Zechariah says: Many nations, he says, shall flee to the Lord, and shall be his people (Zech 2:11). Or, as some will have it, the remnant of believers from Israel is called the people; and the tribe, or nations, are those who believed from the multitude of the nations, as Moses says to the nations in the Song of Deuteronomy: Rejoice, you nations, with his people (Deut 32:43). For tribe, as we have translated, Theodotion translated race, Symmachus nation, the Seventy kings. For we are the tribe, and the nation, and the royal and priestly race of the Lord, such as Abraham also was, who was called a king, and the other saints, of whom it is written: Do not touch my anointed ones (Ps 104 [105]:15). What is it that they are bidden to hear? For a law, he says, shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the peoples, or of the nations. Here is shown the spiritual law of the Gospel, which shall go forth from Zion, not that of Moses, which was given of old on Sinai; and my judgment shall go forth for a light of the nations, by which he established and decreed that all nations are to be saved.

But when the time of his incarnation unexpectedly arrived, then the shadows made way for the truth. And he said, "Listen to me, O my people." … He is speaking here not only to those who are numbered among the people but also to the kings, because he wanted the rulers, the leaders of the people, to receive his message as well.… "The law will go forth from me, and my judgment will be a light to the nations." He refers to the divine and evangelical preaching as "law" here; it is just that it is in a different form now, just as the oracles and salvation also are new. For just as the old law was changed to something better, there has also been a transfer from those things that were provisional types to that which is the truth. For Christ said, "Do not think I have come to destroy the law." … The law in letters was given by Moses, but the preaching of salvation, which is the gospel, came through Christ.… He calls his "judgment" here something that is both sanctioned by the law of God as well as a benevolent accounting; it is the grace from him that went out to illuminate the Gentiles; they were amazed at his judgment, which was both righteous and just—truly the righteousness that is clearly made known in the gospel.

925. Third, he sets out the manner of execution: hearken unto me.

And first, he sets out the divine intention: a law, the precept of Cyrus concerning the liberation of the people; my judgment, promulgated from the justice of the Lord; to be a light, comfort, above: to them that dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, light is risen (Isa 9:2).

And lest perhaps we should think that what he promised would come after a long time, he adds: near is my righteous one, or righteousness. For Christ has been made for us by the Father wisdom and redemption (1 Cor 1), holiness and righteousness, and all the names by which virtue is called. And it is beautifully said that righteousness will go forth, so that not one nation only but the whole world may be saved. And that the Son of God, who was sent by the Father, is called Savior, or salvation, which in Hebrew is said Jesus, Simeon declares, holding the child in his arms: Now you dismiss your servant, O Lord, for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples, a light for the revelation of the nations (Luke 2:29ff.). And as for what follows, And my arms shall judge the peoples, or according to the Seventy, and in my arm shall the nations hope: it signifies either that all are judged by his power, or that all the nations will believe in Christ, who is the arm and strength of God. It is said also in another place: Your arm is with might. Let your hand be strengthened, and your right hand exalted (Ps 88 [89]:14). And again: Sing to the Lord a new song: his right hand will save for him, and his holy arm (Ps 97 [98]:1, 2). For the right hand and arm of the Lord is he himself who saved for himself those who were formerly lost, so that none should perish of those whom the Father had given him (John 17). And that the islands are said to be either the souls of the Saints, which in the persecutions of this world have been made solid by a firm faith in God, or the multitude of the Churches from the nations, we have often explained. And just as by the arm of the Lord we can understand the Savior, so by his arms which judge the peoples we can understand all the saints, in whom God will judge the world.

If we want to know the meaning of these words in the person of God and Father, then we say that he calls the Son "his righteousness." For we are saved in him … through his great mercy.… He is called "righteousness" and "salvation" and rightly so. For he has removed all evil from us and, freeing us from the chains of death, has led us into eternal life.… Those who were once weak and prostrate on the ground grasp his right hand and gain the hope of an unexpected salvation. For the holy Scriptures often call the Son the right arm of the Father. For he is his power.

He calls his power "arm": that which constitutes the greatest proof of divine power is to have conquered the world by the cross, by ignominy and by death; it is to have given fishermen, publicans, shoemakers as masters to philosophers and to rhetoricians; it is to have, thanks to a dozen men, cultivated the whole world and, thanks to an equally small number of men, filled the entire earth and sea with the divine message.

Second, he sets out the nearness of the judgment: my just one is near at hand, namely, Cyrus, or Christ; my savior is gone forth, already in my foreknowledge, above: I have brought my justice near (Isa 46:13).

Third, he sets out the usefulness of the judgment: arms, powerful men, by my power, Cyrus and Darius; the islands shall look for me, various peoples will hope in me, seeing the liberation of the people, above: he will set judgment in the earth (Isa 42:4).

Again, as to their malignantly asserting that if heaven is indeed the throne of God, and earth His footstool, and if it is declared that the heaven and earth shall pass away, then when these pass away the God who sitteth above must also pass away, and therefore He cannot be the God who is over all; in the first place, they are ignorant what the expression means, that heaven is [His] throne and earth [His] footstool. For they do not know what God is, but they imagine that He sits after the fashion of a man, and is contained within bounds, but does not contain. And they are also unacquainted with [the meaning of] the passing away of the heaven and earth; but Paul was not ignorant of it when he declared, "For the figure of this world passeth away." In the next place, David explains their question, for he says that when the fashion of this world passes away, not only shall God remain, but His servants also, expressing himself thus in the 101st Psalm: "In the beginning, Thou, O Lord, hast founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of Thy hands. They shall perish, but Thou shalt endure, and all shall wax old as a garment; and as a vesture Thou shalt change them, and they shall be changed: but Thou art the same, and Thy years shall not fail. The children of Thy servants shall continue, and their seed shall be established for ever;" pointing out plainly what things they are that pass away, and who it is that doth endure for ever—God, together with His servants. And in like manner Esaias says: "Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look upon the earth beneath; for the heaven has been set together as smoke, and the earth shall wax old like a garment, and they who dwell therein shall die in like manner. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not pass away."

But if our opponents say, How then is it, if the universe is not destroyed, that the Lord says that "heaven and earth shall pass away," and the prophet, that "the heaven shall perish as smoke" and "the earth shall grow old as a garment"; we answer, because it is usual for the Scriptures to call the change of the world from its present condition to a better and more glorious one destruction, as its earlier form is lost in the change of all things to a state of greater splendor, for there is neither contradiction nor absurdity in the Scriptures. For not "the world" but "the fashion of this world" passes away, it is said. So it is usual for the Scriptures to call the change from an earlier form to a better and more comely state "destruction"; just as when one calls by the name of "destruction" the change from a childish form into a perfect adult, as the stature of the child is turned into mature size and beauty.

But, however, we say thus: That which our Redeemer said to us is true:—Heaven and earth shall pass away. And the Apostle said, Hope which is seen is not hope. And the Prophet said, The heavens shall pass away as smoke, and the earth as a garment shall wear away; and its inhabitants shall become like it. And Job said concerning those that sleep, Till the heavens wear out, they shall not be aroused, nor shall they wake out of their sleep. From these things be thou persuaded that this earth, in which the children of Adam are sown, and the firmament that is over men, (even) that firmament which is set to divide the upper heavens from the earth and this life, shall pass away, and wear out, and be destroyed. And God will make a new thing for the children of Adam, and they shall inherit inheritances in the Kingdom of Heaven. If He shall give them inheritance in the earth, it shall be called the kingdom of heaven. And if in Heaven, it is easy for Him to do.
Demonstration 22 (Of Death and the Latter Times), Section 24

Upon the essence of the heavens we are contented with what Isaiah says, for, in simple language, he gives us sufficient idea of their nature, “The heaven was made like smoke,” that is to say, He created a subtle substance, without solidity or density, from which to form the heavens. As to the form of them we also content ourselves with the language of the same prophet, when praising God “that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in.”
The Hexaemeron, Homily 1: In the Beginning God Made the Heaven and the Earth

Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath: for the heavens shall melt away like smoke, and the earth shall be worn away like a garment, and its inhabitants shall perish like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. LXX: Lift up your eyes to heaven, and look upon the earth beneath, for heaven has been made firm like smoke. But the earth shall grow old like a garment, and its inhabitants shall die like these. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness shall not fail. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away (Matt 24:35). And David sings in the psalm: In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment; and like a cloak you shall roll them up, and they shall be changed (Ps 101 [102]:26). From this it is shown that the perishing of the heavens signifies not destruction but a change for the better. Of these it is said: There shall be a new heaven and a new earth, which I will make to remain in my sight (Rev 21:2). For if it is written of the saints, We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed (1 Cor 15:51), and in the titles of four psalms we read, For those who shall be changed: how much more is this to be believed of heaven and of the sun and the stars, when the moon shall receive the light of the sun, and the sun shall glow with sevenfold brightness? Hence the whole creation too groans and travails, awaiting the revelation of the sons of God, that it may be changed for the better (Rom 8). And not only the souls of men, which are immortal, but their bodies too are to be changed into a glorified substance. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality (1 Cor 15:53). And since heaven and earth grow old, it follows that the things contained within the circle of heaven, and men, who are the inhabitants of the earth, also die like these: not unto their destruction, but unto the abolishing of their old baseness and the renewal of the glory to come; when the righteous shall shine like the sun (Matt 13:43), and, the past and old things departing, all things shall have been made new. Some take perishing and growing old for abolition and death, according to what we read in the catholic Epistle: The heavens that now are, and the earth, have been reserved for fire by the same word. And again: The elements, burning, shall be dissolved (2 Pet 3:7). This is indeed also the opinion of the philosophers of the world, that all the things we see will perish by fire. Hence the Apostle too: Passes away, he says, the fashion of this world, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal (1 Cor 7:32). Something of the kind the apostle John also writes: The world passes away, and its desire (1 John 2:17). And in the Hebrew it is said, The heavens shall melt away like smoke; or, according to Aquila and Symmachus, they shall be ground to nothing, and be crumbled and vanish in the manner of salt; of whom the former said ἡλίσθησαν, the latter ἁλίσουσιν, which plainly draws its etymology from the crumbling and dissolving of salt. In place of this I wonder what the Seventy meant to say, heaven has been made firm like smoke: for if firmness is taken for strength, how is what is firm compared to smoke? Unless perhaps we can say this: that all the firmness and strength and might of the heavens is made equal to the emptiest wind and to smoke, which dissolves into the air, according to Ecclesiastes: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity (Eccl 1:2). And this must be said: if heaven and earth shall perish and grow old, by what consequence should its inhabitants die and perish like these, when we know that souls are everlasting, and that bodies will rise again? From this it is plain that heaven and earth do not perish and are not reduced to nothing, but are changed for the better.

The Son is called "salvation" and "righteousness," as we often say, and thus his quality is declared that he has in himself, by which and in which he is Son by nature. Indeed, he is eternal and does not "wear out." Such is the difference between creator and creation, the made from the maker, which is clearly seen in this verse.

From the sky and the earth, from the things on high and those below, learn of my power. I produced these elements with great ease and, conversely, I can make them disappear. "But my salvation shall be for eternity, and my righteousness shall not fail." This is what the Lord has likewise said in the holy Gospels: "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words will by no means pass away."

926. Lift up your eyes to heaven. Here he shows the firmness of the divine promise by comparison to the changing of creatures.

Hence he first sets out the changeableness of creation: the earth shall vanish, as to shape and as to substance (1 Cor 7:31); and the same thing is to be said concerning the others: in the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth: and the heavens are the works of your hands (Ps 101:26[102:25]).

Second, the firmness of the divine promise: but my salvation shall be for ever, because I promise it, or because I will never lack, so as to not be prepared to save and do justice: heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away (Luke 21:33).

Hear me, you who know what is just, people: my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. For as a garment, so shall the worm eat them; and as wool, so shall the moth devour them. But my salvation shall be for ever, and my righteousness to generations of generations. LXX: Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, of whom my law is in their heart. Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their contempt. For like a garment they shall be consumed by time, and like wool they shall be eaten by the moth. But my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation to generations of generations. He who had said above, A law shall go forth from me, and my judgment for a light of the nations, now speaks to the same people, who know his judgment and have his law in their hearts, that they may do all things with judgment, and have the law which the Lord promises through Jeremiah, saying (Jer 31:31ff.): I will establish a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers; but I will establish a covenant, putting my laws in their minds, and upon their heart I will write them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people: so that they may live by no means according to the letter but according to the spirit, restoring the natural law in their hearts, of which the Apostle also writes: For when the nations, which do not have the law, do by nature the things that are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; who show the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom 2:14). Of this law it is signified in the psalm: The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted (Ps 36 [37]:30, 31). And because the prophetic spirit knew that many persecutions would come upon believers, he exhorts them to fortitude, nay rather to contempt of those who are going to persecute them. Which the Lord also said in the Gospel: Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; but rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matt 10:28). And in another place: Rejoice when they speak all evil against you, lying (ibid. 5:11).

This is what the Lord has also said in the divine Gospels: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul," and again: "Do not fear them," and: "Blessed are you when they revile and persecute you and shall say all kinds of evil against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven." Similarly, here, the prophetic text has shown that people who revile and trample underfoot the heralds of truth are like garments and like wool that is eaten away by the moth, while the salvation and the righteousness of those who are being insulted has no end and escapes death. After having made the prediction here concerning the new people, [the prophet] passes to another subject and prophesies to Jerusalem the return from exile in Babylon. One should know, however, that these announcements were not made at the same time as the others, but that the first dates from one epoch, the second from some other time, and that they were put together later to form a single book.

927. Hearken to me. Here he excludes the impediment which could be feared from oppression, so far as pertains to the power of their oppressors. And concerning this, he does two things:

first, the consolation of the Lord is set out;

second, the discussion of the prophet: arise (Isa 51:9).

Concerning the first, he does four things.

First, he stirs up attention: you that know what is just, that is, the justice which I have revealed in my judgments: he has not done in like manner to every nation: and his judgments he has not made manifest to them (Ps 147:20); in your heart, in your understanding: let them not depart from your eyes, keep them in the midst of your heart (Prov 4:21).

Second, he excludes fear: fear not the reproach of men, who hold you in contempt, glorying in their own power: but I am a worm, and no man: the reproach of men, and the outcast of the people (Ps 21:7[22:6]).

For as a garment is consumed by the worm, or by time, and as wool is devoured by the moth, so all the reproach of the persecutors will pass away with the persecutors. Hence the Apostles too gloried that they had been counted worthy to suffer insults for the Lord (Acts 5). And they gloried because the salvation and righteousness of the Lord, which had promised them victory and rewards, that is, the Lord and Savior, abides for ever, or in each generation, of the former people and of the later, who received his coming; of whom it is also said above: Near is my righteous one, my savior has gone forth.

Third, he shows their fragility: for the worm shall eat them up as a garment: who am as a garment that is moth-eaten (Job 13:28).

Fourth, the firmness of divine help: but my salvation shall be for ever, above: Israel is saved in the Lord with an eternal salvation (Isa 45:17).

According to the Hebrew, it is not Jerusalem but the arm of the Lord that has to put on strength. This relates to what we spoke about above [v. 5], about the nations hoping in "my arm." For we have said that the divinity of the Word is signified here, since he urges the people not to fear the rebuke of human beings or to be affected by their filth, and in the same way here it is right to see in the person of the people a prayer being sent to the "arm of the Lord" to rouse himself and overcome the enemies of his people. For we confess we are nothing unless you rise up and overcome on our behalf.

Arise, arise; put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the days of old, in the generations of ages. Was it not you who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty deep, who made the depth of the sea a way, that the freed might pass over? And now those who have been redeemed by the Lord shall return and come into Zion praising; and everlasting gladness shall be upon their heads: they shall hold joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning shall flee. LXX: Rise up, rise up ÷ Jerusalem ⁚ and put on the strength of your arm. Rise up as in the beginning of the day, as an everlasting generation. Are you not she who cut down the breadth, who undid the dragon? Are you not she who made the sea a desert, the many waters of the deep; who made the depth of the sea a way of passage for those who had been freed and redeemed? For by the Lord they shall be led back, and shall come into Zion with gladness and everlasting exultation. For on their head praise and gladness shall take hold of them. Sorrow and grief and groaning shall flee. The name Jerusalem, which was added here by the Seventy, is neither found in the Hebrew nor did any of the three Translators put it; hence it is to be marked beforehand with an obelus, and so the following little chapter is to be joined with the sense of the preceding. The Lord had exhorted those who believe in him, saying: Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be afraid of their blasphemies. And he had promised them, as their help, his salvation and everlasting righteousness, which is none other than Christ, the arm of the Lord, of whom he had said above: And in my arm shall the nations hope. Hence the people speak to the arm of the Lord, and pray for his coming, and implore the promised help, saying: Arise, arise: put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Arise as in the days of old, and exert all your strength, so that you who through many ages delivered your Saints from dangers may protect us too by your strength. For you are he who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon, namely Pharaoh king of Egypt, who in Ezekiel too is called the great dragon (Ezek 29). You dried up the Red Sea, so that through the most mighty waters and the depths of the sea your people might find a way and escape the pursuing Egyptians. You, then, who did these things, now too lead back into Zion those redeemed and freed by your blood, into the heavenly Jerusalem, or into the Church which you have prepared for yourself by your blood: and when they are in it, they shall rejoice with everlasting gladness, and shall say: Lord, as with the shield of your good will you have crowned us (Ps 5:13). For they shall have joy and gladness, sorrow and groaning fleeing away. This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Seventy, Jerusalem, that is, the sinful soul, is called to put on the strength of her arm, and to take up her former works, as she had been before she fell, when she dwelt in the day and in the light. For you are she, he says, who overcame the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and broke up the dragon, the crooked serpent, of which we also read in the Psalms: You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters (Ps 73 [74]:13). Remember your former strength, that you trod down the sea of this world and made it a desert, and found a way in the midst of the waves.
